title: Good-deed compositions written with his aunt
summary: Green explains compositions of good deeds, his aunt tutoring him and his grandmother's strictness.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Would you -- can we just go back a second? You're talking about getting up in front of the class and doing composition. What kind of composition would you do for the class, and what exactly was a composition?
Was it a song? Was it a dance? What -- what --

Well, it was mostly similar to a song, but it was like something that you did during the day when you were away from school, you see, and like at that time they had something -- way of -- but you'd have to be a certain age. You'd have to do 13 good deeds a day, and, you know, as I would say it, see, one of my mother's mother's daughter was a teacher. She was learning to be a teacher at the time. That's the one that taught me to do the time step. She also played the piano. My mother did too, of course, and Self Approval -- was one of the compositions that I used to talk, you see, about a good deed. You know, I tried it. I'd help old people cross the street, you know, help the blind, you know, anyone, do errands, anything, something that's a good deed, considered a good deed. Now, if you do 13 good deeds, that's supposed to have been some kind of a credit for you, like there was being a Boy Scout, becoming a Boy Scout, see. So that's what my mother's mother used to tell me, how she'd -- how she'd write it down, pencil and paper, you know, and how to explain it, about the good deeds that I had did during the day. And she said, by the way, says, 'I have something for you to do, and you know I'm an old woman because I'm your mother's mother, you know. And your mother too.' You know, she was -- I liked to call her grandmother, you know, but
she didn't prefer that, you know. And I tried to make her laugh, you see. But it was very hard. She was a tough audience, you see.

But she was a good woman. She was a good human being. And she taught me how to count my blessings. I'll say it thataway, as for respectful. So she said I should write down these good deeds that I do, and being head of the class, she said, let's put it down. And my daughter, when she gets home, she will tell you how to put it on paper where you can get up and explain it.

And she would say, 'you can read your own writing, can't you?' And I said, 'yes, ma'am,' you know, said -- so that's really what happened. When my Aunt E(unintelligible)came home, she would teach me how to explain these good deeds, you see? So like healping an old person on to the streetcar --
So let us continue. The floor is yours, Chuck.
